name: Calf implants

lead: Calf implants are silicone prostheses placed under the fascia or muscle of the lower leg to add volume. People use them for thin calves that do not respond to training, for asymmetry or wasting, and bodybuilders seek them for size. The payoff is larger, more muscular-looking calves.

Implants were first reported in 1979. Surgeons have published single-center series and a 2019 review pooling 26 studies on 1,498 patients and 2,629 calves. Fat grafting and combined approaches are also described as alternatives. The evidence is surgeon-reported case series and reviews rather than controlled trials, and looksmaxxing forum discussion is limited.

paras: A surgeon makes an incision, typically behind the knee, and places a solid or gel-filled silicone implant beneath the fascia or in a plane between the calf muscles. The added volume shows after healing, with a period of restricted activity beforehand.

The 26-study review analysed complication rates by technique. Reported problems include seroma, implant displacement, capsular contracture, dissatisfaction leading to removal and, in one case, acute compartment syndrome with muscle necrosis. Regulation of implants and surgeons varies by country.

angle.text: A silicone implant placed in the calf adds lower-leg volume for larger, more muscular-looking calves, visible after healing. Evidence comes from surgical case series and a 26-study review.

lead: Calf augmentation is a cosmetic and reconstructive surgery that adds volume to the lower leg, most often with a silicone implant placed beneath the fascia or between the calf muscles, and sometimes with fat grafting. [1][2] Indications in the surgical literature include thin or underdeveloped legs, asymmetry, bodybuilders who want more muscle size, and deformity left by injury, illness or a congenital condition. [1][2]

The appearance payoff is direct and structural: the implant adds volume and projection where the muscle is thin, so the lower leg looks fuller from the front and the side and sits in better proportion with the thighs in shorts or swimwear. Patients who describe skinny calves despite training are a recurring group in both surgeon reports and press coverage. [1][3]

The first reports date to the 1970s: a 1979 report of silicone-gel implants is cited in a surgical review, and early designs were followed by firmer silicone rubber implants and, later, placement in the plane between the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles. [4] Surgeons have published single-center series, a 25-year experience paper, and a 2019 review pooling 26 studies covering 1,498 patients and 2,629 calves. [2][5][6]

Published evidence consists of case series and reviews; no randomized trials were found. In bodybuilding and looksmaxxing communities the procedure is a niche topic, usually raised by people whose calves stay small despite training, and in popular culture it has been a recurring comedy reference. [7][3]

paras: Implants are made of solid semisoft silicone, which can be carved to fit, or of a firm shell containing cohesive silicone. [8] A 2000 report favoured soft silicone implants as more natural-looking than hard ones, placed over the gastrocnemius or beneath the fascia through an incision at the popliteal crease. [9]

A submuscular approach, between the gastrocnemius and soleus, was developed because subfascial implants had visible capsular contracture problems and firm implants could be felt through the skin. [4] A 2009 anthropometric study classified calf defects into five types to guide implant type, size and plane. [10] Fat grafting for calf augmentation has been reported as an alternative to silicone implants, and combined composite augmentation in staged procedures has been described. [11][12]

A 2009 anthropometric study looked at 2,600 photographs of standing women and took calf measurements in 168 women aged 15 to 61, to define the features that make calves look attractive and to catalogue defects into five types that guide implant selection [10]. A 25-year experience paper pairs surgical results with an anatomical review of the region [5]. Surgeons also describe operating on under-developed calves after treatment of congenital clubfoot deformity, a reconstructive use [13].

The surgical literature describes three broad groups of patients. Aesthetic patients have naturally slim or underdeveloped lower legs. Reconstructive patients have a deformity after injury, illness or a congenital condition. A third group is made up of bodybuilders and other athletes whose calves remain small relative to the rest of the physique. [1] In the 1991 to 2016 series, 23 of 50 patients were treated for aesthetic reasons, six were bodybuilders and 21 had lower-leg reconstruction after illness-related deformity, an unusually high proportion of reconstructive cases for a calf series. [1]

Series differ in who they treat. A Stockholm series of 18 patients had 13 women and five men, while a 2000 series of 100 patients had 95 women and five men. [8][9] The authors of a 2019 review of 26 studies note that attention to calf appearance has been growing in both men and women, and they analysed demographics, including age and gender, alongside complication rates. [2]

Surgeons also describe calf appearance in terms of proportion. The 2009 anthropometric study measured the legs of 168 women aged 15 to 61 to identify front-to-back and side-to-side projection ratios that consistently make legs look attractive, and it sorted calf defects into five types that guide the choice of implant design, size and plane. [10] Implants can also be used for asymmetry, where one calf is smaller than the other. [9]

Cleveland Clinic describes calf implants as an outpatient procedure in which a plastic surgeon places the implant through a small incision behind the knee, usually under general anaesthesia. It lists medical-grade silicone, solid or gel-filled, as the usual material, and distinguishes subcutaneous placement (less invasive, faster recovery, but more prone to shifting and visibility) from submuscular placement (longer recovery, a more natural look). [14]

A 2018 MEL Magazine feature quoted Toronto surgeon Marc DuPere as saying that the patient lies face down and a roughly two-inch incision behind the knee leads to a pocket over the gastrocnemius, which has medial and lateral heads that the implant is shaped to mimic. He said about three quarters of his male patients receive one implant per leg, with two per leg typical for bodybuilders. [3]

Recovery accounts describe several days of pain, swelling and soreness, with Cleveland Clinic putting a return to work at about two weeks, most activities at about six weeks and full resolution of swelling at several months. [14] The MEL feature reported crutches for one to two weeks, a week or more off work and a pause on driving because the calf muscles operate the pedals. [3] Cleveland Clinic describes ideal candidates as adults who already strength train, do not smoke and have realistic expectations. [14]

The Aesthetic Society reports an average cost of $5,026 for calf implant surgery, based on 2021 Aesthetic Plastic Surgery National Databank statistics; the figure covers surgeon and facility fees and may exclude anaesthesia, tests, prescriptions and surgical garments. [15] The MEL feature cited US averages of $4,500 to $6,000 and a Canadian surgeon's all-inclusive fee of about Can$12,000 for both legs. [3]

The first implants were placed below the deep fascia of the calf, and later surgeons described moving the implant into the plane between the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles to hide the edges of firm implants and reduce capsular problems. [4] The senior author of the 2017 series reports introducing technical modifications over a 25-year experience, including a purpose-designed inserter instrument for placing calf implants. [1][5]

Fat grafting is described as an autologous alternative that avoids a foreign implant and lets the surgeon shape the medial and lateral calf separately. [11] Composite augmentation combines an implant with fat grafting in a staged procedure, and its authors stress anatomical features and health conditions that affect safety. [12] Surgeons have also applied calf augmentation to under-developed calves left after treatment of congenital clubfoot. [13]

No randomized trials were identified. Evidence consists of case series and reviews. A 2017 series covering 1991-2016 included 50 patients who had 60 calf corrections, 23 aesthetic and 21 reconstructive; the surgeon rated results excellent-to-good in 30 of 37 followed patients and patients rated results very good in 18, good in 10, acceptable in 7 and bad in 2. [1]

A 2000 series of 100 patients (200 implants) reported no infections, ruptures or hematomas, four seromas that resolved, and removal of four implants in two dissatisfied patients. [9] A 2005 report described 18 patients at a Stockholm clinic, and a 2017 study examined the safety and efficacy of subfascial augmentation. [8][16]
A 2019 review analysed complication rates for subfascial implants, submuscular implants and fat grafting across 26 studies from 1993 to 2018. [2]

The 2000 series operated on 100 patients (95 women and 5 men) between 1985 and 1999, using mainly soft Glitzenstein implants, and its author reported that patients walked about eight hours after surgery and that no functional problem or muscular dysfunction had been seen [9]. A report on fat grafting for calf augmentation and reshaping presents an autologous alternative to silicone [11].

The 2019 review by Melita and Innocenti (Aesthetic Plastic Surgery) covered 26 studies from 1993 to 2018. Per its reported figures, subfascial implants (1,929 calves) had a complication rate of 5.7%, submuscular implants (435 calves) 0.92% and fat grafting (265 calves) 1.5%, with an overall rate of about 4.5%. The authors described complication rates as low compared with other body contouring procedures, noted high patient satisfaction, observed that fat grafting had low complication rates but needs multiple sessions, and recommended experienced plastic surgeons. [2][6]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: Calf implants appear in forum talk mostly as a half-serious fallback for genetically small calves. On T Nation a member writes that they would "totally get calf implants" once they are big but still stuck with small calves [7]. Other posts mention implants in passing, including a poster who recalls a television programme about a man who had calf, pectoral and gluteal implants, and a remark that a female bodybuilder obtained calf implants to match large thighs [17][18].
These are anecdotes rather than data. The surgical literature describes bodybuilders among the patients who seek the procedure [1].

MEL Magazine (2018) traced calf implants as a running joke in television and stand-up, naming a 2014 Modern Family episode and jokes by Conan O'Brien in 2010 and Amy Schumer in 2016, with screenwriter Dode Levenson calling the gag an offshoot of the breast-implant joke. [3]

The same article profiled patients, including a 33-year-old Canadian who had implants after a social media comment about skinny calves and said training had not changed them. DuPere said his calf-implant patients split evenly between women and men and linked rising male interest to social media photos; Eppley said he was not aware of recent gay male patients, while other sources in the piece described calf implants as popular among gay men. [3]

In the 2017 series, one 28-year-old professional bodybuilder developed acute anterior compartment syndrome in one leg; the implants were removed after 16 hours but muscle ischaemia and necrosis followed, requiring several operations. [1] Other reported issues include seroma, implant displacement and capsular contracture. [9][4] Anatomical and physiological considerations, including some health conditions, are cited as relevant to safety in staged composite augmentation. [12]

Cleveland Clinic lists possible complications as implant leakage or rupture (gel implants), shifting or a palpable edge, capsular contracture, infection, bleeding, bruising, blood clots, nerve damage or numbness, muscle spasms and skin changes, and says serious problems are uncommon. [14] Indianapolis surgeon Barry Eppley told MEL that early implants of unusual materials placed in 1968 produced complications in one patient about 40 years later, and that licensed implants have been available in the US since the mid-1990s. [3]

lore.intro: Calf implants come up on bodybuilding forums as an option for people whose calves resist growth, mentioned in passing rather than as a developed topic [7][17].
